questions.title: Customer Order Analysis
questions.intro: You have two tables: customers and orders.
task: Find customers who have at least 2 Delivered orders.
Only count orders with amount >= 500.
Display customer_name, delivered_orders and total_amount.
Sort by total_amount descending.
questions.hint: Join the two tables using customer_id. Filter rows before grouping; use HAVING for the minimum order count.
questions.solution:
SELECT c.name AS customer_name,
       COUNT(*) AS delivered_orders,
       SUM(o.amount) AS total_amount
FROM orders o
JOIN customers c ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id
WHERE o.status = 'Delivered' AND o.amount >= 500
GROUP BY c.customer_id, c.name
HAVING COUNT(*) >= 2
ORDER BY total_amount DESC;
steps: JOIN matches every order to its customer.
WHERE removes Cancelled orders (102 and 109) and orders below 500.
GROUP BY customer_id and name forms a distinct group per customer.
COUNT(*) and SUM(amount) produce Asha (2, 2800), Kiran (2, 1600), Meera (1, 2500), Rahul (2, 1100).
HAVING removes Meera because she has only one qualifying order.
ORDER BY sorts the remaining customers by total_amount descending.
questions.initial:
SELECT c.name as customer_name, COUNT(*) AS delivered_orders, SUM(o.amount) AS total_amount
FROM orders o
LEFT JOIN customers c ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id
WHERE o.status = 'Delivered' AND o.amount >= 500
GROUP BY c.name, c.customer_id
HAVING COUNT(*) >= 2
ORDER BY SUM(o.amount) DESC

checks.error: Join the orders and customers tables.
Keep only customers with at least two orders.

questions.title: Employee Salary Update
questions.intro: You have the following employees table.
task: Write ONE UPDATE statement.
Increase salary by 20% for Backend employees with 3 or more years of experience.
Increase salary by 10% for Backend employees with less than 3 years of experience.
Do not modify employees from other departments.
questions.hint: Use UPDATE ... SET salary = CASE WHEN ... THEN ... ELSE ... END WHERE ...
questions.solution:
UPDATE employees
SET salary = CASE
    WHEN experience >= 3 THEN salary * 1.20
    ELSE salary * 1.10
END
WHERE department = 'Backend';
steps: UPDATE identifies the employees table.
WHERE restricts changes to the Backend department.
CASE evaluates each selected employee's experience.
Priya and Sneha get 20% increases; Rahul gets a 10% increase.
All QA and DevOps salaries remain unchanged.
questions.initial:
UPDATE employees 
SET salary = CASE 
       WHEN experience >= 3 THEN salary + (salary * 0.2)
       ELSE salary + (salary * 0.1)
END
WHERE department = 'Backend'

questions.title: Create & Insert Courses
questions.intro: Create a new courses table using the schema below and insert two courses.
task: Create courses with all four columns and the specified constraints.
Insert SQL Basics (1500) and DSA (2000) in ONE INSERT statement.
Do not manually specify course_id or is_active.
Write both the CREATE TABLE and INSERT statements.
questions.note: Expected IDs assume a fresh table with default auto-increment settings.
questions.hint: AUTO_INCREMENT generates IDs. DEFAULT TRUE supplies the active flag when omitted. Multiple VALUES tuples can be inserted with one INSERT.
steps: CREATE TABLE defines the four columns and their constraints.
AUTO_INCREMENT creates IDs; UNIQUE and NOT NULL enforce data rules.
The INSERT specifies only course_name and fee.
VALUES supplies two rows, so MySQL creates them in one statement.
With a fresh table, IDs are 1 and 2, and is_active defaults to 1.
questions.initial:
CREATE TABLE courses (
       course_id INT AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY,
       course_name VARCHAR(100) UNIQUE NOT NULL,

)

Add is_active BOOLEAN NOT NULL DEFAULT TRUE.

questions.title: Warehouse Restock Queue
questions.intro: The products table contains current stock and the minimum reorder level for each product. Only active products should appear in the restock queue.
task: Write a SELECT query to list products that need restocking.
Include only active products (is_active = 1) whose stock is strictly below reorder_level.
Display product_name, stock, and a computed column named shortage, equal to reorder_level - stock.
Order by shortage from highest to lowest. When shortages tie, order by product_name alphabetically.
questions.hint: Filter active items and compare stock against reorder_level in WHERE. Give the difference an alias, then sort using that alias.
questions.solution:
SELECT product_name, stock, reorder_level - stock AS shortage
FROM products
WHERE is_active = 1 AND stock < reorder_level
ORDER BY shortage DESC, product_name ASC;
steps: Look at each product's is_active flag. Remove USB Hub because it is inactive.
Compare stock with reorder_level for the remaining products. Mouse, Laptop and Headphones are not below their reorder levels.
Calculate shortage for the four remaining products: Keyboard 10-5=5, Monitor 5-2=3, Webcam 8-0=8, Charger 5-1=4.
Sort shortage descending to get Webcam, Keyboard, Charger, then Monitor. Product name is the tie-breaker if equal shortages occur.
questions.initial:
SELECT product_name, stock, (reorder_level - stock) AS shortage
FROM products
WHERE is_active = 1 AND stock < reorder_level
ORDER BY shortage DESC, product_name ASC

checks.error: Only include products whose stock is below the reorder level.
Calculate shortage as reorder_level - stock and name it shortage.
Sort the restock queue by shortage descending and product_name ascending.

questions.title: Students Without a Passed Exam
questions.intro: Every student is listed in students. The exam_attempts table records zero or more exam attempts per student. A student may have only failures, at least one pass, or no attempts at all.
task: Use a correlated NOT EXISTS subquery to find students who have never passed any exam.
A student with no exam attempts must also appear in the result.
Display student_id and student_name.
Order results alphabetically by student_name.
questions.hint: For each student, ask whether there exists a matching exam_attempts row with result = 'Pass'. Keep the student when no such row exists.
questions.solution:
SELECT s.student_id, s.student_name
FROM students AS s
WHERE NOT EXISTS (
    SELECT 1
    FROM exam_attempts AS a
    WHERE a.student_id = s.student_id
      AND a.result = 'Pass'
)
ORDER BY s.student_name ASC;
steps: Start with all six rows in students; the outer query considers them one at a time.
For Anaya, the subquery finds a DBMS Pass, so NOT EXISTS is false and Anaya is removed.
For Bharat, both attempts are Fail. The subquery finds no Pass, so Bharat remains.
For Charu and Dev, each has a Pass and is removed.
Esha has no attempt rows at all. There is no Pass, so NOT EXISTS is true and Esha remains.
Farhan has one Fail and no Pass, so Farhan remains.
ORDER BY student_name ASC yields Bharat, Esha, and Farhan.

checks.error: Use a NOT EXISTS correlated subquery.
Check whether a student has a Pass attempt.

questions.title: Latest Two Payments Per Customer
questions.intro: Each row in payments represents a separate payment. A customer can have more than two payments or only one payment, and multiple payments can happen on the same date.
task: Find the two most recent payments for each customer using ROW_NUMBER() and a CTE (WITH clause).
Within each customer, treat a later payment_date as newer. If two payments share the same date, treat the higher payment_id as newer.
Customers with fewer than two payments should still appear with all their payments.
Display customer_id, payment_id, payment_date, and amount; do not display the row number.
Sort the final result by customer_id ascending, payment_date descending, then payment_id descending.
questions.hint: In a CTE, use ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY payment_date DESC, payment_id DESC). Then filter the numbered rows in an outer SELECT.
questions.solution:
WITH ranked_payments AS (
    SELECT payment_id, customer_id, payment_date, amount,
           ROW_NUMBER() OVER (
               PARTITION BY customer_id
               ORDER BY payment_date DESC, payment_id DESC
           ) AS rn
    FROM payments
)
SELECT customer_id, payment_id, payment_date, amount
FROM ranked_payments
WHERE rn <= 2
ORDER BY customer_id ASC, payment_date DESC, payment_id DESC;
steps: The CTE reads every payment and groups rows into independent partitions by customer_id.
ROW_NUMBER() sorts each customer's rows by date descending and breaks same-date ties using payment_id descending.
Customer 1 receives row numbers 1 for payment 103, 2 for 102, and 3 for 101. Payment 103 is first because 103 is higher than 102 on the same date.
Customer 2 receives row numbers 1 for 202 and 2 for 201. Customer 3 has only payment 301, numbered 1.
Customer 4 receives row numbers 1 for 404, 2 for 403, 3 for 402, and 4 for 401.
The outer query keeps row numbers 1 and 2, removes the rn column from display, and sorts the remaining seven rows in the requested order.

checks.error: Sort by newest payment date first.
For equal dates, order by payment_id descending.
Filter to the first two row numbers in the outer query.

questions.title: Subscription Payment Summary
questions.intro: A subscription service records every payment attempt. A payment can be Success, Failed, or Pending. Prepare a summary for each plan without losing plans that have no successful payments.
task: Write one SELECT query returning exactly one row per plan_name.
Display plan_name, total_attempts (count all rows), failed_attempts (count only status = 'Failed'), and successful_amount (sum amount only when status = 'Success').
Use CASE-based conditional aggregation for failed_attempts and successful_amount. Failed and Pending amounts must not contribute to successful_amount.
Include plans with zero successes; their successful_amount must be 0.
Sort by successful_amount descending, then plan_name ascending.
questions.hint: GROUP BY plan_name. COUNT(*) includes every attempt. Use SUM(CASE WHEN ... THEN ... ELSE 0 END) for each condition; do not filter statuses in WHERE.
questions.solution:
SELECT plan_name,
       COUNT(*) AS total_attempts,
       SUM(CASE WHEN status = 'Failed' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS failed_attempts,
       SUM(CASE WHEN status = 'Success' THEN amount ELSE 0 END) AS successful_amount
FROM subscription_payments
GROUP BY plan_name
ORDER BY successful_amount DESC, plan_name ASC;
steps: GROUP BY plan_name creates four groups: Basic, Pro, Premium, Starter.
COUNT(*) counts all attempts, including Pending and Failed: Basic 3, Pro 4, Premium 3, Starter 2.
For each row, the Failed CASE returns 1 only for Failed; summing gives one failed attempt in each plan.
For each row, the Success CASE contributes the amount only for Success. Premium: 1500+1000=2500; Pro: 700+500=1200; Basic: 200; Starter: 0.
Sorting by successful_amount descending gives Premium, Pro, Basic, Starter. The name is the tie-breaker for equal totals.

checks.error: Count all attempts, including Pending and Failed.
Count failures with CASE-based conditional aggregation.
Sum successful payments with CASE-based conditional aggregation.
Use SUM for the conditional totals.
Sort by successful_amount descending, then plan_name ascending.

questions.title: Movies Above Their Genre Average
questions.intro: A movie catalog stores each movie's genre and rating. Compare a movie's rating against the average rating of all movies in its own genre (including itself). A genre may contain only one movie.
task: Use a correlated scalar subquery with AVG() to find movies rated strictly above the average rating of movies in the same genre.
Calculate the average using all movies in that genre, including the movie currently being checked.
Display only title, genre, and rating.
Exclude movies whose ratings equal their genre average. A single-movie genre therefore produces no result.
Sort by genre ascending, then rating descending, then title ascending.
questions.hint: For each outer movie row, run SELECT AVG(rating) on another alias of movies, restricted to the same genre, and compare the outer rating with >.
questions.solution:
SELECT m.title, m.genre, m.rating
FROM movies AS m
WHERE m.rating > (
    SELECT AVG(m2.rating)
    FROM movies AS m2
    WHERE m2.genre = m.genre
)
ORDER BY m.genre ASC, m.rating DESC, m.title ASC;
steps: The outer query checks each movie one by one.
The correlated subquery computes an average for the current movie's genre. Sci-Fi average is (7+9+8)/3 = 8; Comedy average is (6+8)/2 = 7.
Drama average is 8, and both Drama movies equal it, so neither qualifies.
Thriller average is (8.5+9+7.5)/3 = 25/3 ≈ 8.33. Deep Line (8.5) and Night Signal (9) are above it.
Documentary contains one movie rated 9.5; its average is 9.5, so Solo Act is not strictly above it.
The qualified rows are Sunny Days, Orbit Nine, Night Signal, and Deep Line; ORDER BY puts them in the requested genre and rating order.

checks.error: Calculate each genre's average with AVG().
Filter movies by comparing their rating with a subquery.
Use a scalar SELECT AVG(...) subquery.
Correlate the inner genre with the outer movie's genre.
Sort by genre, rating, and title as specified.

questions.title: Daily Paid Revenue Running Total
questions.intro: A sales platform records purchases at different stores. Multiple paid purchases can occur at the same store on the same date. Failed and Refunded purchases do not count toward revenue.
task: Use a CTE to calculate daily_revenue as the sum of amounts for Paid sales on each store_id and sale_date.
Exclude Failed and Refunded sales entirely. Days with no Paid sales should not appear; stores without any Paid sales should not appear.
In the outer query, use SUM(...) OVER (...) to calculate running_revenue for each store, in sale_date order, including the current day's daily_revenue.
Display store_id, sale_date, daily_revenue, and running_revenue.
Sort the final output by store_id ascending, then sale_date ascending.
questions.hint: First build a daily_paid CTE with WHERE status='Paid' and GROUP BY store_id, sale_date. Then run SUM(daily_revenue) OVER (PARTITION BY store_id ORDER BY sale_date ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW).
questions.solution:
WITH daily_paid AS (
    SELECT store_id, sale_date, SUM(amount) AS daily_revenue
    FROM sales
    WHERE status = 'Paid'
    GROUP BY store_id, sale_date
)
SELECT store_id, sale_date, daily_revenue,
       SUM(daily_revenue) OVER (
           PARTITION BY store_id
           ORDER BY sale_date
           ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW
       ) AS running_revenue
FROM daily_paid
ORDER BY store_id ASC, sale_date ASC;
steps: Inside the CTE, WHERE status = 'Paid' removes sale IDs 3, 8, 10, 11 and 13 before adding amounts.
The CTE groups multiple purchases from the same store on the same date. For store 1 on Nov 1, 100+200 gives daily_revenue 300.
The daily revenue for store 1 is 300 (Nov 1), 150 (Nov 2), and 300 (Nov 4). Store 2 has 400 (Nov 1), 200 (Nov 3), and 50 (Nov 5). Store 3 has only 500 (Nov 4).
The window function PARTITION BY store_id restarts the total for each store, and ORDER BY sale_date adds each day's revenue in chronological order.
Store 1 running totals are 300, 450, 750. Store 2 totals are 400, 600, 650. Store 3 has 500.
Store 4 has no paid purchases, so it never enters the CTE. The final ORDER BY lists each store's dates from oldest to newest.

checks.error: Use a CTE to compute daily revenue first.
Group by store and sale date before the running total.
Use SUM(daily_revenue) OVER (...) for the running total.
Restart running totals separately for each store.

questions.title: Department Headcount and Payroll
questions.intro: A company stores departments separately from employees. Some departments may have no employees yet. Build a summary that includes every department, even an empty one.
task: Write one SELECT query that displays every department, including departments with zero employees.
Show department_name, employee_count (number of employees), and total_payroll (sum of employee salaries).
For departments with no employees, employee_count and total_payroll must both be 0, not NULL.
Sort by total_payroll descending. Break ties with department_name ascending.
questions.hint: Start from departments, not employees. Think about which JOIN preserves rows with no matches, and which COUNT expression avoids counting a placeholder NULL row.
questions.solution:
SELECT d.department_name,
       COUNT(e.employee_id) AS employee_count,
       COALESCE(SUM(e.salary), 0) AS total_payroll
FROM departments d
LEFT JOIN employees e ON d.department_id = e.department_id
GROUP BY d.department_id, d.department_name
ORDER BY total_payroll DESC, d.department_name ASC;
steps: Start with all five rows of departments. LEFT JOIN matches employees to each department, while preserving Legal even though it has no employee match.
Group by department_id and department_name, so one summary row is produced per department.
COUNT(e.employee_id) counts actual matching employees. For Legal it counts 0 because the unmatched employee_id is NULL.
SUM(e.salary) adds salaries: Engineering 90000 + 110000 = 200000; Operations 60000 + 60000 + 60000 = 180000; Support 50000 + 45000 = 95000; Design 72000.
Legal's SUM is NULL, so COALESCE turns its total_payroll into 0.
Sort by total_payroll descending and by department_name ascending for ties.

checks.error: Start from departments to include all of them.
Include departments even when no employee matches.
Count the employees in each department.
Return 0 instead of NULL for empty department payrolls.
Sort by descending payroll, then department name.

questions.title: Apply Category Discounts with UPDATE JOIN
questions.intro: A store maintains product prices and category-wide discount rules in separate tables. Apply qualifying discounts to product prices directly in the products table.
task: Write ONE MySQL 8.0 UPDATE statement using a JOIN between products and category_discounts on category_id.
Reduce a product's current price by its category discount_percent, but ONLY when the product is active, the category discount is enabled, and discount_percent > 0.
Round every changed price to two decimal places using ROUND(..., 2). Assume price is stored as DECIMAL(10,2).
Leave all other products unchanged. Do not manually calculate or hardcode individual new prices.
questions.note: Expected result is the price table after running the UPDATE exactly once; display prices to two decimal places.
questions.hint: MySQL supports UPDATE table_alias JOIN other_table ON ... SET ... WHERE ... . Use the discount as a percentage of the existing price and filter out inactive products and disabled/zero discounts.
questions.solution:
UPDATE products p
JOIN category_discounts d ON p.category_id = d.category_id
SET p.price = ROUND(p.price * (1 - d.discount_percent / 100), 2)
WHERE p.is_active = 1
  AND d.enabled = 1
  AND d.discount_percent > 0;
steps: Match each product to its category discount row using category_id.
Filter: products 2 and 7 are inactive; category Home is disabled (product 3); Clothing has 0% discount (product 5). These prices are unchanged.
Notebook becomes ROUND(99.99 × 0.85, 2) = ROUND(84.9915, 2) = 84.99.
Only Charger, Novel, Notebook and Tablet are updated. The remaining four products keep their original prices.

checks.error: Assign the new price in SET.
Round changed prices to two decimals.

questions.title: Weekly Revenue Change Using LAG
questions.intro: A retailer stores individual sales transactions. Compute each store's total completed revenue for each recorded week and compare it with the previous week that had completed sales.
task: Use a CTE (WITH clause) to calculate weekly_revenue = SUM(amount) for only Completed sales, grouped by store_id and week_start.

Using LAG() OVER (PARTITION BY store_id ORDER BY week_start), calculate previous_revenue from the previous RECORDED week with completed sales for the same store (not necessarily the immediately preceding calendar week).
Calculate revenue_change = weekly_revenue - previous_revenue. For a store's first recorded completed-sales week, both previous_revenue and revenue_change must be NULL.
Exclude weeks with zero Completed sales; exclude stores with no Completed sales.
Display store_id, week_start, weekly_revenue, previous_revenue, revenue_change, and order by store_id ascending and week_start ascending.
questions.note: NULL values in the expected output are SQL NULL values, not the text 'NULL'. Store 2 has no Completed sales in the week of 2026-10-12, so the 2026-10-19 row compares to 2026-10-05.
questions.hint: Aggregate first, then apply LAG to the aggregated rows—not to individual transactions. You can use a second CTE so that revenue_change can reuse the previous_revenue alias.
questions.solution:
WITH weekly_sales AS (
    SELECT store_id, week_start, SUM(amount) AS weekly_revenue
    FROM sales
    WHERE status = 'Completed'
    GROUP BY store_id, week_start
), weekly_with_previous AS (
    SELECT store_id,
           week_start,
           weekly_revenue,
           LAG(weekly_revenue) OVER (
               PARTITION BY store_id
               ORDER BY week_start
           ) AS previous_revenue
    FROM weekly_sales
)
SELECT store_id,
       week_start,
       weekly_revenue,
       previous_revenue,
       weekly_revenue - previous_revenue AS revenue_change
FROM weekly_with_previous
ORDER BY store_id ASC, week_start ASC;
steps: WHERE status = 'Completed' removes the Cancelled, Refunded and Pending transactions. Store 4 disappears because it has no Completed sales.
GROUP BY store_id, week_start sums completed transactions for each week: store 1 has 500, 450, 675; store 2 has 700, 650, 750; store 3 has 1000, 900.
LAG(weekly_revenue) processes the aggregated weeks within each store in week_start order; for store 1 the prior values are NULL, 500, 450.
For store 2, the Refunded-only 2026-10-12 week is absent. The 2026-10-19 row therefore compares its 650 against 700 from 2026-10-05.
Subtract previous_revenue from weekly_revenue: store 1 gives NULL, -50, 225; store 2 gives NULL, -50, 100; store 3 gives NULL, -100.
For the first row of each store, LAG returns NULL and the subtraction also stays NULL. Final ORDER BY gives store_id and chronological week order.

checks.error: Use a CTE to aggregate weekly sales.
Group transactions by store and week.
Use LAG to retrieve previous recorded weekly revenue.
Calculate LAG independently for each store.
Order each store's window by week_start.
